- File: scripts/files_touched_scope_guard.py
  Line or code reference: lines 153-155 (entry_matches function)
  Problem: When an allowlist entry ends with "/" (e.g., "frontend/"), the implementation returns `path == prefix or path.startswith(entry)` where prefix is entry[:-1]. This means a directory-prefix entry like "frontend/" also matches a bare file literally named "frontend". The module-level docstring at lines 42-44 documents only the subdirectory behavior ("frontend/ allows frontend/anything"), not this bare-file match. The test `test_directory_prefix_entry_matches` at test file line 86 explicitly asserts this lenient behavior is IN_SCOPE by passing staged path "frontend" alongside an allowlist entry of "frontend/", confirming the implementation is intentional but the docstring is misleading.
  Why it fails at runtime: If a staged file is literally named "frontend" (possible from a symlink, rename, or directory-to-file type change), a "frontend/" allowlist entry meant to scope work only to files inside the directory would incorrectly accept it. This weakens the incident-protection intent described in the PR (blocking compiled twins and out-of-scope drift). The directory-prefix semantics for the "/" form should either be restricted to `path.startswith(entry)` only (dropping the `path == prefix` clause) to match the docstring, or the docstring should be updated to document the lenient behavior.
  ISSUE_CONFIDENCE: 4
- File: scripts/files_touched_scope_guard.py
  Line or code reference: line 206 (_read_staged function)
  Problem: `_read_staged()` normalizes line endings with `text.replace("\r\n", "\n").split("\n")`. The same file's `extract_files_touched()` at line 95 already uses Python's built-in `text.splitlines()`, which handles all line-ending variants (\r\n, \r, \n) automatically and is the standard Python idiom. The manual approach is redundant, less readable, and does not handle \r-only line endings (old Mac style).
  Why it fails at runtime: On Linux CI runners where git always produces \n line endings via `git diff --cached --name-only`, this is not a runtime bug today. It is a code-quality inconsistency within the same module — the same file uses `splitlines()` in one function and manual replacement in another. Risk of actual failure is very low.
  ISSUE_CONFIDENCE: 3
